meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nothing can be more contrary to religion and the clergy than reason and common sense'?
meta.ogDescription: Misattributed to Voltaire. It's Baron d'Holbach, Théologie portative (1768) — and even the English wording is a paraphrase of his French.

answer.label: Not Voltaire — actually Baron d'Holbach
answer.sourceLine: This is not Voltaire. The epigram is a loose English rendering of a line by Baron d’Holbach in his satirical Théologie portative, ou Dictionnaire abrégé de la religion chrétienne (1768), under the entry Folie: “Rien n’est plus contraire à la Religion et au Clergé qu’une tête sensée et raisonnable” — literally “a sensible and reasonable mind,” not “reason and common sense.” Wikiquote files the line among Voltaire’s misattributed quotations ↗.

source.heading: The real source: d’Holbach’s satirical dictionary

docMeta.dd: Théologie portative, ou Dictionnaire abrégé de la religion chrétienne
Paul-Henri Thiry, Baron d’Holbach (published pseudonymously as “abbé Bernier”)
Popular English is an anonymous loose rendering; d’Holbach’s French reads “une tête sensée et raisonnable” (a sensible and reasonable mind)

source.excerpt: Folie. Les bons Chrétiens se glorifient de la folie de la Croix. Rien n’est plus contraire à la Religion et au Clergé qu’une tête sensée et raisonnable ; elle n’est jamais bien propre à la foi, ni assez susceptible de ferveur ou de zèle.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Voltaire — Misattributed section ↗, crediting Baron d’Holbach, Théologie portative (1768), entry “Folie.”

We confirmed the exact French against the full Théologie portative text (Les Classiques des sciences sociales, UQÀM) ↗: “Rien n’est plus contraire à la Religion et au Clergé qu’une tête sensée et raisonnable.”
Quote sites such as BuboQuote ↗ print it under Voltaire with no source — the pattern of a famous name absorbing a lesser-known contemporary’s line.
source.excerptNote: From the entry “Folie” (Folly). Literally: “Nothing is more contrary to Religion and the Clergy than a sensible and reasonable mind; it is never well suited to faith, nor susceptible enough to fervour or zeal.” The circulating English swaps “a sensible and reasonable mind” for “reason and common sense.”

source.rightsNote: The source work, d’Holbach’s Théologie portative, was first published in 1768 and is long in the public domain; the circulating English is a loose modern paraphrase of that public-domain French text, carrying no separate protected translation.

author.name: Paul-Henri Thiry, Baron d’Holbach
author.heading: About Baron d’Holbach
author.bio: Paul-Henri Thiry, Baron d’Holbach (1723–1789) was a German-born, French-naturalized philosopher whose Paris salon hosted Diderot, Hume, Adam Smith and Benjamin Franklin. A contributor to the Encyclopédie, he became the most uncompromising atheist and materialist of the Enlightenment, author of the Système de la nature (1770). He published his anticlerical works — including the satirical Théologie portative — anonymously or under borrowed names to evade censorship, which is partly why his sharpest lines drift to more famous signatures like Voltaire’s.

misattribution.heading: Why it’s pinned on Voltaire
misattribution.intro: The quip is anticlerical, epigrammatic and 18th-century French — a perfect fit for Voltaire’s reputation. But it belongs to his contemporary Baron d’Holbach, and even the familiar English wording departs from what d’Holbach actually wrote.

items.why: Quote sites, image memes and databases print the line under Voltaire with no citation. Wikiquote places it in its Voltaire Misattributed section ↗ and points instead to d’Holbach. Ironically, Voltaire publicly opposed d’Holbach’s atheism (in the article “Dieu” of his own Dictionnaire philosophique).
d’Holbach wrote “une tête sensée et raisonnable” — “a sensible and reasonable mind” — which the popular English compresses into “reason and common sense,” confirmable in the 1768 text ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Baron d’Holbach, in Théologie portative (1768), entry “Folie” — and the English is a loose paraphrase of his French, per Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: An Enlightenment barb, mis-signed
lead: d’Holbach’s Théologie portative is a mock “pocket theology” — a dictionary that defines Christian terms with deadpan irony to expose what he saw as their absurdity. Under “Folie” (Folly) he needles the celebrated “folly of the Cross,” arguing that a clear, rational mind is precisely what faith and clergy cannot abide.

Because d’Holbach published such works anonymously to dodge censorship, his sharpest lines circulated unsigned — easy to later re-file under the era’s most famous freethinker. The mislabeling is doubly ironic: Voltaire, a deist, actually took up his pen against d’Holbach’s outright atheism.
context.pull: A rational mind, d’Holbach jokes, is the last thing religion and the clergy can tolerate.
